issues.explanation: For a natural disaster trauma in a 34-year-old Navy Officer, 'Known People: Related people' is hard to reconcile as a trauma-linked trigger without any accompanying memory or appraisal content about bereavement, loss of specific others, or interpersonal aspects of the disaster. The rest of the profile does not explain why related people would be a salient trigger.

issues.item: Avoid Evaluation: Situations in which other people evaluate me / my appearance / my performance
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Evaluation' is poorly matched to the rest of the profile. It suggests social/performance shame concerns, but the negative appraisals and memory items do not involve appearance, performance failure, humiliation, or social judgment. This maladaptive strategy appears to address a symptom theme not otherwise represented.

'Avoid Friends' similarly implies socially driven withdrawal, yet the selected appraisals are global despair and alienation rather than fear of specific interpersonal consequences, and the trigger set does not include friendship or social contact themes. It is not impossible, but in combination with 'Avoid Evaluation' it pulls toward a social-evaluative formulation not supported elsewhere.

For a natural-disaster trauma in a Navy officer, 'Similar cars' is hard to connect clinically to the rest of the profile. The other triggers are generic situational reminders (crowding, locations), but this item implies a specific vehicle-related cue that is not supported by the trauma type, memory content, or appraisals.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Life Not Worth Living: I am not sure my life is worth living anymore
issues.explanation: The negative appraisals are extremely global and severe ('life not worth living', 'belong nowhere') relative to the rest of the selected items, which focus on trauma reminders, fragmented imagery, and avoidance. This creates a coherence problem because the profile lacks corresponding threat content or broader self-concept material to support such pervasive suicidal/existential beliefs.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere
issues.explanation: 'I no longer belong anywhere' is especially difficult to reconcile with the demographic/contextual profile of a married Navy officer after a natural disaster unless other items indicate moral injury, social alienation, or occupational rupture; none are present in the selected components.

vignette: Jonathan is a 34-year-old Navy Officer who has been struggling with symptoms following a traumatic natural disaster that occurred during his deployment. The event was intense and overwhelming; he found himself trapped in a small space amidst the chaos of hurricane-force winds and flooding waters. The experience left him feeling utterly helpless and alone, despite being surrounded by fellow service members. Since then, Jonathan has found himself avoiding crowded places and any physical locations reminiscent of the disaster. Even the smell of alcohol—a memory associated with celebratory drinks before the storm—triggers a sense of unease that plunges him back into the trauma. These triggers have led him to isolate himself further from friends and family, as he believes seeing them will inevitably lead to another triggering moment. Jonathan's memories are vivid and visceral; when they come to mind, his body physically reenacts the position he was in during the event. He often finds himself reliving the experience with such clarity that it feels unreal, as if it could not have actually happened to him. This bodily reenactment exacerbates his sense of isolation, making him feel that he no longer belongs anywhere. Jonathan has come to believe that he deserves to suffer because of what happened and that there is a reason for his pain. These negative appraisals have reinforced the idea that he should avoid situations that remind him of the disaster, further isolating himself from friends and family. His maladaptive thinking has deepened his sense of loss; he used to be a happy person but now feels perpetually miserable. Jonathan's avoidance behaviors have concrete consequences in both his personal life and his work. He often skips social gatherings with colleagues and avoids bars or parties where the smell of alcohol might trigger memories. This behavior has led to strained relationships, as friends find it hard to understand why he is so distant and avoidant. At work, Jonathan’s performance has been affected by his inability to be in certain environments; he finds himself withdrawing from situations that require teamwork. His negative appraisals have also fueled a cycle of avoidance and maladaptive thinking. He feels isolated and set apart from others because these memories keep coming back with such force that it seems impossible for him to lead a normal life. The memory of being trapped in the hurricane has seeped into his daily routine, making him hyper-aware of potential triggers that could bring on another flood of emotions. Jonathan’s belief that he deserves to suffer makes him more likely to relive these memories and experience their vividness. He feels as if there is no escape from the trauma; it haunts him in every aspect of life. This cycle has tightened over time, making Jonathan feel increasingly trapped by his own thoughts and reactions. What finally brought Jonathan to seek help was a profound realization that he could not continue living this way. He was most afraid of losing himself completely to these memories and negative appraisals, but at the same time, he hoped for a chance to reclaim some sense of normalcy and happiness in his life.
